edges.relationship: Farge credits Foucault’s writings with turning her historical practice toward ruptures and discontinuities, and his analysis of power with opening an inquiry into popular opinion.
edges.evidence_note: Farge’s own 2012 answer identifies the effect on her practice. Her 17 June 1997 interview specifies La Volonté de savoir and Surveiller et punir when explaining the archival investigation behind Dire et mal dire. This is an acknowledged resource, distinct from joint authorship and from her particular disagreement over presenting documents. The complete cited books were not freshly read.

edges.relationship: Farge recalls opposing Foucault’s initial wish to present the documents for Le Désordre des familles without commentary: their aesthetic force still required historical explanation.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2001 recollection of their work on the jointly credited 1982 book. She explicitly shares his emotional response to the documents; the disagreement concerns their initial presentation. It establishes neither a rejection of Foucault nor the book’s final division of labor. The original editorial conversation and complete book remain unread.

edges.relationship: Farge explicitly uses Bourdieu’s Méditations pascaliennes to examine bodies as sites where political power is inscribed and collective action becomes possible.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2001 response about bodily experience names this particular analytical resource. The book itself remains unread in this dossier. Her specific criticism of La Domination masculine is separately retained; use of one argument does not establish agreement with all of Bourdieu’s work.

edges.relationship: Farge includes Bourdieu’s La Domination masculine in her criticism of accounts that make gender domination invariant, while directing the sharper objection at Françoise Héritier.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2001 answer contrasts historical movement with invariance and names Bourdieu’s 1998 book. The main target remains Héritier’s Masculin/Féminin; she is not replaced by Bourdieu. Existing field edge 1402 already preserves that broader intervention and remains unchanged. Neither original book was freshly read.

edges.relationship: Farge identifies Habermas’s account of a repressed plebeian public sphere as an intellectual stimulus for investigating popular political judgment in Dire et mal dire.
edges.evidence_note: Own interview dated Paris, 17 June 1997, preserved in the publisher’s public article record. She calls Habermas’s formulation a stimulus while explaining the different historical investigation it prompted. Complete L’Espace public and Dire et mal dire were not read here. The resource coexists with her explicit historical objections.

edges.relationship: Farge challenges a history of public opinion that leaves popular judgment uncultured or merely repressed and makes change descend continuously from the literate bourgeois sphere.
edges.evidence_note: Her 17 June 1997 answers explicitly limit this to historical inquiry, disclaiming a direct philosophical critique of Habermas. She investigates changing practices, intermediate relays and discontinuities. This does not assert that Habermas denied every plebeian sphere. The response is read in the publisher’s transcription, not the complete 1992 monograph; the transmission contains unresolved corruptions outside the cited sentences.

edges.relationship: In her 2013 foreword, Davis treats Farge’s account of archival work as a guide that deepens her own understanding of research, interpretation and the material encounter with documents.
edges.evidence_note: Davis’s own selected foreword, especially xii–xv, not evidence of formative influence on her earlier career. Her coediting recollection on x establishes collaboration without causal priority. Thomas Scott-Railton translated Farge’s 1989 book; Davis wrote the separate 2013 foreword. The legal preview ends during xv; the complete foreword and Farge’s book body remain unread.

edges.relationship: Bailyn identifies Pocock’s research among the resources used to reconstruct the British opposition traditions in revolutionary American thought.
edges.evidence_note: The foreword reproduced in the 1992 enlarged edition, printed xii, explicitly places Pocock with other British political-thought researchers. Robbins, Gough, Laslett, Weston and other named scholars retain their distinct credit; no sole-source or general Cambridge-school lineage is asserted. The original 1967 copy and Pocock’s cited works were not collated or freshly read.

edges.relationship: Wood recalls Bailyn’s seminar teaching him historical-mindedness as a way of understanding rather than accumulating facts.
edges.evidence_note: Wood’s own 2021 interview answer describes his 1958 seminar experience and its intellectual effect. This supports a specific acknowledged teaching debt, without treating all students as a school or assigning Wood the separate recollections of Brown and Allison. No verbatim seminar record or complete later work was read.

edges.relationship: Bailyn praises Braudel’s descriptions but argues that separated temporal layers cannot by themselves explain historical interaction and change.
edges.evidence_note: Own December 1981 address, published February 1982: the Braudel paragraphs and note 8 criticize the architecture of the Mediterranean study while valuing its evidence. This is Bailyn’s particular methodological judgment, not a rejection of every Annales historian. His earlier 1951 review and Braudel’s complete book were not freshly read.

edges.relationship: Bailyn agrees with much of Stone’s narrative-revival account but argues for an explicitly evaluative synthesis that incorporates analytical history.
edges.evidence_note: In note 10 of the 1981/1982 address, Bailyn distinguishes his aim from Stone’s account of changing fashion and qualifies any opposition between narrative and analysis. Agreement remains explicit. He states that he read Stone after drafting, so this passage is not made an influence claim. Existing collective route 672, from contextual history to Stone, remains unchanged.

edges.relationship: Colley values Bailyn’s Atlantic connections but challenges strong claims for their regional unity and the exclusion of early Asian connections.
edges.evidence_note: Her 2006 review distinguishes praise for Atlantic inquiry from criticism of Bailyn’s stronger geographical model. The unity discussion at the end of section 1 and Asia discussion at the end of section 2 support this limited objection. Pestana’s book is separately reviewed; its claims are not silently assigned to Bailyn. No blanket rejection of Atlantic history or fresh reading of Bailyn’s whole 2005 book is asserted.

edges.relationship: Bailyn credits Calloway’s account of Indigenous devastation but disputes its broad framing of the Revolution against earlier British imperial violence and Enlightenment aspirations.
edges.evidence_note: Own 1995 review: opening assessment, village-study qualifications and final contextual argument. Praise and disagreement coexist. Bailyn’s contextual defense and judgments about Britain, the Revolution and Enlightenment ideals remain his claims; they are not editorial findings that dispose of Calloway’s argument. Calloway’s whole book and any reply were not read.

edges.relationship: As Rakove explains, Morgan’s account of the Stamp Act crisis supplied a basis that Bailyn extended through radical Whig ideology and changing colonial self-understanding.
edges.evidence_note: Explicit named scholarly mediation: Rakove’s 2020/2021 memorial discussion of Ideological Origins identifies the resource and two additions. The original Morgan studies remain unread here; this route claims neither sole authorship of the underlying research nor an exclusive source for Bailyn. It does not substitute Rakove’s absent individual endpoint or create a biography.

edges.relationship: As Ian Davey reads the 1988 schooling study, Curtis combines Foucault’s analysis of power and subjectivity with a Marxist account of state formation.
edges.evidence_note: Explicit named scholarly mediation: Davey’s 1989 review, printed 161, identifies the combination as an analytical strength, while his criticism of patriarchal relations on 165 remains. Curtis’s complete 1988 book and the particular Foucault originals remain unread; this is a specified theoretical resource, not an exclusive lineage or unqualified agreement.

edges.relationship: Palmer questions treating Curtis’s school-inspection study as a representative model of Canadian state formation, while crediting its revision of responsible government.
edges.evidence_note: Fresh primary review, 1993, printed 365–367: Palmer finds the inspection focus too narrow and its model overstated, but acknowledges useful evidence and the responsible-government argument. His separate criticism of Greer and Radforth’s edited collection retains its own subject; the entire joint review is not assigned to Curtis. Curtis’s 1992 book remains unread.

edges.relationship: As Christie and Fecteau report, Curtis questions McKay’s singular liberal project and recommends closer attention to governmentality.
edges.evidence_note: Explicit named mediation: Christie’s 2009 essay, paragraph beginning Since liberalism, attributes the governmentality point to Curtis without identifying his text. Fecteau’s 2009 discussion quotes Curtis’s objections to deterministic identity/action and a unitary project, citing 179 and 184. Curtis’s chapter and McKay’s full reply remain unread; these witnesses are consolidated rather than counted as separate exchanges.

edges.relationship: Curtis credits Elias’s work with shaping his interpretation of state paper collections.
edges.evidence_note: Undated first-person Carleton research statement, About, paragraph beginning Historians criticized. Other credited resources remain distinct; no particular Elias title, edition or date of transmission is supplied.

edges.relationship: Curtis names Marx’s sociology among the resources directing his attention to changing social forms and practices.
edges.evidence_note: Undated first-person Carleton statement, About, paragraph beginning Together with. Simmel, Bourdieu and the previously named resources share credit; this does not make Curtis’s approach wholly Marx’s.

edges.relationship: Curtis identifies Bourdieu’s sociology and category slippage as resources for studying social forms and classification.
edges.evidence_note: Undated first-person Carleton statement, About, paragraphs beginning Together with and I have always. This credits specific analytical interests; the original Bourdieu works remain unread and unnamed.

edges.relationship: Curtis objects that political authorities cannot simply discover population, because population depends on the exercise of sovereign authority.
edges.evidence_note: The substantive authorial abstract of Curtis’s 2002 article, reproduced on ResearchGate, reconstructs Foucault’s usage and states this conceptual objection. Reading is limited to the English/French abstract; the complete article and Foucault originals remain unread. This specific criticism coexists with the separately evidenced Foucault resource and does not establish wholesale rejection.

edges.relationship: Armitage credits Bayly with formative questions and continuing support for the doctoral research that became The Ideological Origins of the British Empire.
edges.evidence_note: Own acknowledgments x name Bayly with Burke, Collinson, Hont and Pagden; all retain credit. The preceding Princeton group and later examiners are distinct. This records specified research support, not sole supervision or a known particular question. Full monograph unread.

edges.relationship: Bayly adapts Appadurai’s vocabulary of cultural mixing and the absorption of earlier connections to analyse archaic and early capitalist globalization.
edges.evidence_note: Own publisher sample p.44 explicitly credits Appadurai for ethnoscape and cannibalizing. This is specified analytical use, not general personal influence. Appadurai’s original work, book notes and the complete Bayly monograph remain unread.

edges.relationship: Bayly uses de Vries’s industrious revolutions to describe regional changes in production and consumption that new globalizing powers sought to connect and exploit.
edges.evidence_note: Own chapter1 pp.44–45 names de Vries and retains uneven change and persistent bodily practices. This particular resource is distinct from the p.40 reference to the first modern economy, whose joint-book credit was not checked. Neither all of de Vries’s account nor a sole economic cause is asserted.

edges.relationship: Hall welcomes Bayly’s global connections but argues that power, gender and racial difference need a more sustained role in his account of modernity.
edges.evidence_note: Hall’s own review, especially its final four substantive paragraphs in the full institutional archive. She seeks to enrich the analysis alongside states and war; her praise and specific criticism coexist. The current RiH extraction ends earlier. No Bayly reply found; full book unread.

edges.relationship: As Chakrabarty reproduces Bayly’s 1988 assessment, Bayly questions whether Guha’s approach makes peasant consciousness too unified and unchanging.
edges.evidence_note: Explicit Chakrabarty mediation through the2016 tribute, quoting Bayly1988 pp.114–115. The original review and Guha monograph were not freshly read. Amin is separately discussed, not identified with Guha. Existing mixed357/976 retain the broader collective debate; this adds the specifically named personal criticism.

edges.relationship: Chakrabarty argues that Bayly mistook Subaltern Studies’ use of structuralist analysis for essentialism or Orientalism, while recognizing Bayly’s later openness to dialogue.
edges.evidence_note: Own retrospective tribute, read in an attributed courtesy reproduction; publisher PDF uncollated. This records Chakrabarty’s criticism and later qualification, not adjudication of every original essay or a unified Subaltern Studies position. Guha and Amin retain distinct authorship.

edges.relationship: Chakrabarty credits Bayly’s reconstruction of eighteenth-century India as a resource for his teaching and recalls their later exchange of drafts and Bayly’s press reading.
edges.evidence_note: Own retrospective tribute: Chakrabarty identifies Bayly’s picture of the eighteenth century as central to his teaching, and separately names shared drafts and Bayly’s press reading for The Calling of History. Read in an attributed courtesy reproduction, uncollated to journal PDF. This consolidates specified uses and assistance, not sole authorship or a one-way lineage. Full books and reader report unread.

edges.relationship: As Catherine Hall reports, Bayly criticizes James Scott for overstating state authority and relying too heavily on official records.
edges.evidence_note: Explicit Hall mediation: her full archived review paragraph on state and society names James Scott separately from users of Foucault. The original book passage and Scott’s works remain unread here. This particular criticism does not establish rejection of all Scott’s scholarship or identify him with Joan Scott.

edges.relationship: Uses Bloch’s account of history’s analytical youth and uncertainty to defend continued methodological self-examination.
edges.evidence_note: Selected published address associated with delivery in1969, concluding paragraphs and notes54/56/58. The notes cite a1964 English edition of The Historian’s Craft; its pages and the French original were not freshly read. This is a particular methodological resource, not a general Annales lineage.

edges.relationship: Uses Kuhn’s account of common scientific paradigms to distinguish historians’ recurrent examination of first principles.
edges.evidence_note: The published address, paragraph beginning Unlike the sciences also and note57, cites The Structure of Scientific Revolutions(1962),162. Woodward doubts history will gain the same release from methodological questioning; he does not simply adopt a Kuhnian historical model. The cited book remains unread here.

edges.relationship: Regards White’s charge that historians evade the standards of both art and science as exaggerated and open to reply.
edges.evidence_note: Woodward’s published address explicitly includes the immediately preceding White quotation among criticisms he considers exaggerated, while warning against professional indifference to criticism. Note32 identifies White’s1966 essay. This narrow reservation does not establish rejection of narrative theory or a freshly read rebuttal of White’s complete argument.

edges.relationship: McPherson recalls Woodward commissioning his Oxford History volume, before the assignment changed to the era covered by Battle Cry of Freedom.
edges.evidence_note: McPherson’s own2000 interview with William R.Ferris describes the initial1865–1900 invitation and his requested move to1848–1865 after another contributor fell ill. Editorial contribution is specified; McPherson retains authorship and initiative. This does not make Woodward responsible for every interpretation in the book.

edges.relationship: Joint conception of the Oxford History of the United States provides a shared editorial project.
edges.evidence_note: McPherson’s2000 recollection names both as conceiving a multiauthor series modelled on the Oxford History of England. Undirected editorial overlap, without causal priority or a shared interpretation of every subject. The transcript’s Hofstetter spelling is a variant, not a second historian.

edges.relationship: As Foner recounts, defends the Populists’ corporate critique against Hofstadter’s emphasis on conspiracy and cultural hatreds.
edges.evidence_note: Explicit named scholarly mediation: Foner’s2022 review, paragraphs beginning For decades and It was a book, distinguishes their disagreement from friendship. It also notes Woodward later conceded exaggerating white Populists’ racial egalitarianism. Original exchanges and complete books remain unread; editorial collaboration does not erase this disagreement.

edges.relationship: Questions the comparative scope of Foner’s Reconstruction while praising its achievement and correcting any implication that Foner lacked comparative expertise.
edges.evidence_note: Woodward’s May1988 review urges comparisons with other emancipations; his June correction explicitly credits Foner’s Nothing But Freedom(1983). The criticism concerns the larger book’s scope, not ignorance of comparison. Foner’s books remain unread here; praise, qualification and the correction belong to one bounded critical reception.

edges.relationship: Criticizes Woodward’s earlier tendency to portray African Americans as victims rather than historical agents, while valuing his engaged scholarship.
edges.evidence_note: Foner’s own2022 review contrasts Woodward’s previous writing with later grassroots Reconstruction scholarship and ends by crediting his public achievement. This is a particular historiographical criticism, not dismissal of the whole corpus. Woodward’s original books and Cobb’s complete biography remain unread.

edges.relationship: As Hannah Tandy documents from Woodward’s1938 letter, Black Reconstruction supplied an acknowledged scholarly debt.
edges.evidence_note: Explicit named scholarly mediation: Tandy’s2021 History MA thesis,31 and note85, identifies the3April1938 letter and Woodward’s acknowledgment. UMass metadata corroborates the letter and debt, but the scan could not be read. The complete book and letter remain unread; the proposal does not adopt Tandy’s wider Watson interpretation.

edges.relationship: Uses Higham’s history of the profession to document American historians’ recovery of intellectual confidence after1945.
edges.evidence_note: In the published address associated with1969 delivery, Woodward names Higham’s1965 account and quotes its diagnosis of restored professional self-respect. Notes1/11 credit Higham et al.; Leonard Krieger and Felix Gilbert retain their coauthor credit. The complete1965 book remains unread here; this is a specified historiographical resource, not an exclusive lineage.
